criterion: The title screen, the chapter rack and the chapter reader leave the drawn scene almost empty, with the header, footer and corner controls kept small at the window edges.
evaluation_rule: Chrome here means the site's own controls laid over the drawing: the header with the Doudou Fever wordmark and the chapters and about links, the footer link, the EN | FR language selector, the fullscreen control and the support us tip control. Three large elements belong over the scene and count as part of the design: the read now button on the title screen, the row of chapter sleeves on the rack and the player capsule along the bottom of the reader. Answer the consent strip first. A yes needs every other control on all three screens to sit small against a window edge, leaving the middle of the drawing open. Answer no if a panel, card, sidebar or block of text covers the middle of the scene on any of the three, or if the header or corner controls grow large enough to compete with the drawing.

criterion: The studio console is a plain document application whose screens hold tables, cards and forms on a flat ground.
evaluation_rule: The studio console is the authors' private back office, reached through the studio sign-in page with an author account: overview, volumes, chapter table, chapter and board editors, panel composer, translations, releases, supporters, insights and settings. The panel composer is meant to show a live preview of one panel with a depth ruler and a parallax scrubber, and that framed preview is part of the document. Say yes when every studio screen lays out its tables, cards and forms on a flat, uniform ground and any drawn artwork stays inside the composer's preview frame or small thumbnails. Say no when a studio screen puts the full-window drawn night scene behind its content, shows falling or throwable characters, or runs decorative animation beyond short hover and press feedback.

criterion: On the legal page the header links, wordmark and footer link are a near-black neutral, the EN | FR divider and inactive language button a deep neutral grey, and the page ground a near-white warm neutral with a faint pink tint.
evaluation_rule: Near-black neutral: black or charcoal with no visible colour cast. Deep neutral grey: a dark grey one step lighter than that near-black. Near-white warm neutral: an off-white leaning faintly pink or cream rather than blue or grey. Mark yes only if all three roles hold on the legal page once the consent strip is answered. Mark no if any of those elements takes a colour outside its family, for example a navy header, a grey-blue page ground, or a language divider as dark as the header.

criterion: Across the public pages the one saturated colour is a mid, vivid amber on the thin loading bar.
evaluation_rule: The thin loading bar is the line along the bottom edge that shows while a page or chapter loads after the first visit, for example on opening a chapter from the rack. Saturated means a vivid, strong hue. Pale or muted tints are expected and are not saturated: the pale muted-red curtain that sweeps across on a language switch, the soft orange line on the first-visit loading screen and the pale orange tint of the about page chips. Answer yes when that bottom bar is a vivid amber and no other button, link, strip, chip, curtain or control on the title screen, rack, reader, about page or legal page uses a vivid hue. Answer no when the bar is another colour or grey, or any of those interface elements shows a vivid red, green, blue or other strong hue.

criterion: The public pages or the studio console offer a dark mode or a theme switch.
evaluation_rule: A dark mode is an alternative colour scheme the site switches into, through a toggle or by following the browser's dark-colour preference. Dark grounds designed into single pages are expected and are not a dark mode: the night scene on the title screen, the charcoal loading backdrop, the about page's dark support section and the not-found page's dark gradient. Yes if any public page or studio screen offers a theme or dark-mode toggle, or restyles itself when the browser prefers dark colours. No if the site keeps one colour scheme and offers no such toggle.

criterion: The EN | FR language switch on the public pages sits in a small pill with round ends.
evaluation_rule: The language switch is the EN and FR pair with a divider between them in a corner of every public page. A pill is a capsule whose short ends are full half-circles. Yes if the switch sits in such a pill. No if the switch has square or slightly rounded corners, or has no enclosing shape at all.

criterion: The studio chapter table for Vol. I shows every chapter on one screen in compact, readable rows.
evaluation_rule: The studio chapter table is the list of a volume's chapters in the signed-in studio console, with the columns Number, Title, State, Release, Readiness and Image bytes, and Vol. I holds six chapters. Answer yes when, at an ordinary laptop-sized window, each chapter takes one single-line row with modest padding, all six rows show together with the column headings, and neighbouring rows stay easy to tell apart. Answer no when rows wrap onto several lines, are padded like tall cards so the six rows need scrolling, or are packed so tightly that rows run together.

criterion: Leaving the title screen, the about page or the legal page fades that page out, and the header and footer recolour through a short colour change when the ground beneath turns dark or light.
evaluation_rule: The fade is the outgoing page turning transparent before the next page shows; any easing counts, and the legal page may fade at an even pace. The recolour happens when the ground under the header switches between light and dark, for example going from the chapter rack back to the title screen, or scrolling into the about page's dark support section, where the header and footer turn cream. Yes when each of those three page exits fades out over a short moment and the header and footer colour change blends over a short moment. No when any of those exits cuts straight to the next page, a fade lingers long enough to hold up navigation, or the header or footer colour switches in a single frame.

criterion: In the studio console, buttons such as New volume, New chapter and Run preflight look different when resting, pointed at, pressed, focused and unavailable.
evaluation_rule: Pointed at means the mouse hovers the button; pressed means the mouse button is held down on it; focused means the button was reached with the Tab key; unavailable means the button is disabled and cannot be used; resting is none of these. A yes needs hovering, pressing and tabbing to each named button to give three looks that differ from resting and from one another, and any disabled button in the console to look dimmed. Answer no when any two of those states look identical, or a disabled button looks like an enabled one.

criterion: On the title screen, the chapter rack and the last panel of a chapter, one action is the visually loudest thing: read now, the selected sleeve and the next-track face.
evaluation_rule: The title screen is the site's opening page with a large read now button. The chapter rack lists chapters as sleeves, near-black capsules each holding one chapter's title, with one sleeve selected and facing forward in the middle. The next-track face is the panel that slides across the player capsule at the bottom of the reader once the last panel is reached, labelled next track with the next chapter's title scrolling. Say yes when on each of the three screens that named element draws the eye first, being larger, bolder or higher in contrast than everything else. Say no when any other element on one of those screens is as loud as the named action or louder.

criterion: Lettering over the drawings on the title screen, the chapter rack, the about page's legend section and the not-found page carries a thin outline or sits on a solid ground.
evaluation_rule: The lettering to check is the header links chapters and about, the footer link legal notice & terms of use, the select a chapter heading on the rack, the legend paragraph beginning Doudou is a megalomaniac sheep on the about page, and the Oopsy, page not found line. A thin outline is a narrow contrasting edge traced around each letter; a solid ground is an opaque band or shape directly behind the text. Yes if every one of those texts that sits over a drawing has an outline or a solid ground. No if any of them sits bare on the drawing.

criterion: In the chapter reader, seeded panel pictures and covers are flat drawings coloured by layer role, each with a simple silhouette and the layer identifier stamped in a corner.
evaluation_rule: Each panel is stacked from layers whose identifier ends in a role name, such as back, stage or characters in c1b1p1-back. Flat means one solid fill colour per shape, with no photograph, texture or gradient. Coloured by role means layers with the same role name share one fill colour across panels, and different roles use different colours. The cover is the small picture in the player capsule at the bottom of the reader. A yes needs every panel of chapter 1 to show flat role-coloured shapes with at least one layer identifier such as c1b1p1-back readable in a corner, and the cover to be a flat drawing with a simple silhouette. Answer no when a panel picture is blank, broken, photographic or textured, when a panel shows no readable identifier, or when layers sharing a role name use different colours.

criterion: Icons on the chapter rack, in the reader and on the about page are simple drawn shapes: a pinched play triangle on sleeves and the next-track face, fast-forward marks on the panel arrows, a padlock with a round shackle, four corner arrowheads for fullscreen and a rounded down arrow under Scroll down.
evaluation_rule: A sleeve is one chapter's near-black capsule on the rack; the next-track face is the panel that slides across the reader's bottom player capsule at a chapter's last panel. A pinched play triangle has its back edge bowed inward. A fast-forward mark is a double chevron with a short bar at its leading tip, mirrored for the previous arrow. The padlock shows on locked sleeves, the four arrowheads on the fullscreen control in a window corner, and the down arrow under the Scroll down prompt on the about page. Answer yes when each of those icons has its described shape. Answer no when any of them is drawn as a different shape, such as a plain triangle, a single chevron, a square-shackled padlock or a sharp-angled chevron.

criterion: In the chapter reader, the near layers of a panel slide past faster than the far layers, continuously, keeping a smooth motion as a panel becomes selected.
evaluation_rule: A panel is one camera stop of the chapter, drawn from stacked layers at different depths: near layers are foreground drawings such as the characters, far layers the background. A panel becomes selected when clicked, which flies the view in to frame it. Yes when, as the view travels along the chapter by arrow key, wheel or drag, foreground drawings slide past visibly faster than the background, and clicking a panel keeps that layered motion gliding with no layer jumping. No when all layers move together as one flat picture, far layers outrun near ones, or any layer snaps to a new position when a panel is selected.
